Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA school buses by hour Figure 24 shows the speed bin distributions for the drayage vocation within source type combination-unit short-haul from FleetDNA data. Urban freeways have a weekday peak around 55–60 mph for various hours. Hours around midnight have sharper peaks at 60 mph, likely due to having only a few hours of data tracked at those times of day. There also appears to be a slight lower-speed peak under 10 mph. For urban other roads, there is a stronger low-speed peak around 5–10 mph, possibly because these roads include congestion as trucks wait at the port. Especially for early morning hours, there is also a slight peak around 60 mph. 35 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA drayage vocation of combination-unit short-haul by hour With more weekday data, transfer trucks also display a 60-mph peak for most operating hours on urban freeways (Figure 25). In Figure 26, on urban freeways during the week, food delivery trucks’ speed is concentrated between 50 and 70 mph, peaking at 60 mph. A very minor secondary peak is slightly visible around 20 mph, possibly due to traffic conditions. On weekends, trucks spend slightly more time at this low-speed peak for morning hours while still displaying the 60-mph peak, but sporadic distributions from several hour lines make these trends more difficult to discern. On urban other roads, we see a much milder peak around 50–60 mph for most hours of the day, with much more time spent under 30 mph and rising to a slight peak at 5 mph. On these charts, we also see how less driving data contributes to distributions where trucks spend all their time in a single speed bin. Vehicles are likely performing their delivery routes on roads other than freeways, which would lend itself to the lower-speed distributions seen on these roads. Figure 26. Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA food delivery vocation of single-unit short-haul by hour Also, from the single-unit short-haul source type, parcel delivery vehicles have some peaking around 60 mph on urban freeways and more speeds under 20 mph on urban other roads, as seen in Figure 27. Compared to food delivery vehicles, the parcel delivery vehicles tend to spend less time above 30 mph on urban other roads and more time in the 10- and 15-mph speed bins.
